title: Diagonalization
body:
A square [[Matrix]] $A$ is **diagonalizable** when it can be written

$$
A = PDP^{-1}
$$

with $D$ diagonal. Building $P$ and $D$ is diagonalization, and the recipe is short: **the
columns of $P$ are the eigenvectors of $A$, and the diagonal entries of $D$ are the matching
eigenvalues, in the same order.**

## What it says

Read right to left, as [[Matrix Multiplication]] demands: $P^{-1}$ converts coordinates into the
eigenvector [[Basis]], $D$ scales each axis independently, $P$ converts back. So a diagonalizable
matrix is *nothing but a set of independent stretches*, viewed from an awkward angle.
Diagonalizing is finding the angle it was meant to be viewed from.

That is the general lesson from [[Basis]]: choosing the right coordinate system is how you make
a hard problem easy. This is the cleanest instance of it in the degree.

## When it works

$A$ ($n \times n$) is diagonalizable exactly when it has **$n$ linearly independent
eigenvectors**, since those are what fill the columns of $P$ and $P$ must be invertible.

Two sufficient conditions worth knowing:

- **$n$ distinct eigenvalues** guarantees it, because eigenvectors from distinct eigenvalues are
  always independent.
- **Symmetric** ($A^T = A$) guarantees it, and better: $P$ can be chosen orthogonal, so
  $P^{-1} = P^T$ and the whole thing becomes $A = PDP^T$ with no inverse to compute. That is the
  [[Spectral Theorem]], and it is the version [[Principal Component Analysis|PCA]] uses.

**Repeated eigenvalues are where it can fail.** If an eigenvalue is a root of multiplicity $k$
but its eigenspace has dimension less than $k$, there are not enough independent eigenvectors
and the matrix is **defective**. The standard example:

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Characteristic polynomial $(1-\lambda)^2$, so $\lambda = 1$ twice, but $(A - I) = \begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ has a one-dimensional null space. One eigenvector, two needed, not
diagonalizable. A shear has one fixed direction and no second one.

So: distinct eigenvalues means diagonalizable, but repeated eigenvalues means *check*, not
*fail*. The identity matrix has one eigenvalue repeated $n$ times and is already diagonal.

## Why it is worth doing

**Powers.** This is the immediate payoff:

$$
A^k = (PDP^{-1})^k = PD^kP^{-1}
$$

because the inner $P^{-1}P$ pairs cancel. $D^k$ is just each diagonal entry raised to $k$, so a
hundredth power costs one diagonalization and $n$ scalar exponentiations instead of a hundred
$O(n^3)$ multiplications. Anything iterative reduces to this: Markov chains, population models,
and the closed form for Fibonacci all come out of diagonalizing a $2 \times 2$ or $3 \times 3$.

**Long-run behaviour.** Once $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$, the largest $|\lambda|$ dominates as $k$ grows,
so the system converges to that eigenvector's direction. Whether a process settles, blows up, or
oscillates is read off $D$ without simulating anything.

**Systems of differential equations.** $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ becomes $n$ separate scalar
equations $y_i' = \lambda_i y_i$ in the eigenvector basis, each with the solution
$e^{\lambda_i t}$. Coupling is a coordinate artefact and diagonalizing removes it. This is the
syllabus's "basic science application" and it is picked up properly in
[[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]; see [[Systems of Differential Equations]], where this paragraph is the
entire solution method.

**Matrix functions.** $e^{A} = Pe^{D}P^{-1}$, and likewise for anything defined by a power
series. Applying a scalar function entrywise along the diagonal is the definition that makes
this work.

## Method

1. Find the eigenvalues from $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$
2. Find a [[Basis]] for each eigenspace by solving $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$
3. Count: if the eigenvectors total $n$, build $P$ from them and $D$ from the matching
   eigenvalues; otherwise the matrix is not diagonalizable
4. Check $AP = PD$, which is the same claim as $A = PDP^{-1}$ with no inverse to compute

$P$ is not unique. Reorder its columns and $D$'s diagonal reorders with it, and any eigenvector
can be rescaled.

## Related

- [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] supplies everything this note uses
- [[Basis]] and change of basis is what $P$ is
- [[Matrix Inverse]]: $P$ must be invertible, which is the independence condition restated
- [[Singular Value Decomposition]] is the rectangular generalisation, and
  [[Spectral Theorem|the symmetric case]] is where it comes from. Both are
  [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]]'s
